My team has been working in a way we are calling calling wiki-driven development, where the wiki is written for the human, not the agent and the human uses primarily the wiki to set direction for the agent. items.title: Claude Mods: Flipping the Harness Inside Out
items.text:
Claude Mods: Flipping the Harness Inside Out
For the last few weeks I’ve used Claude Mods to mold Claude Code to my AI engineering workflow. Claude Code is great out of the box, but every engineering workflow is different. Claude Mods let you make Claude Code yours, in the way you want to pay attention. The “paying attention” part is now the most important thing. In a recent Latent Space post, The Evolution of the Agent Harness, I argued that as models absorb more of the harness into their weights, the part that’s left faces the human. It becomes the Attention Interface: the layer that decides when the agent interrupts you, what it shows you, and which decisions it needs you to make. Claude Mods are an early version of the Attention Interface, and one you can shape yourself. Here’s my bet: ultimately, the harness becomes a platform that other companies build on, with models as the engine. v2.1.305
## What's changed

- Added `sandbox.allowNestedUserNamespaces` so sandboxed commands on Linux can create user namespaces (Chromium, rootless podman); this lets them get around the sandbox's file protections
- Added `CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_USAGE_LIMIT_RECHECK_MS` so unattended retry mode (`CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG`) notices a usage limit that was lifted before its reset

- Fixed `/effort` and `/autocompact` settings not applying when the model name differed from a `modelOverrides` value by letter case or a `[1m]` tag
- Fixed new worktrees in a bare repository sometimes starting from local HEAD instead of the default branch, and unchanged subagent worktrees sometimes not being cleaned up
- Fixed Bash commands on a full disk failing with a raw `ENOSPC` file path: the error now says the disk is full and that nothing ran

items.title: Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
items.text:
Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones (play it here). Unlike my previous experiments, this one is actually fun to play. I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Update: Online multiplayer support Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer. I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop

items.text:
Show HN: Gauge CLI – Open-Source Hillclimbing for Agent Experience
Hi HN! We're releasing an open-source CLI for hillclimbing Agent Experience. That means optimizing your agent-facing surfaces (Skills, CLIs, SDKs, and docs) so that your users' coding agents can easily use your product. Pointing your own agent at the repo is enough to get started. https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cliWe've found that power users generally want to hand a CLI/MCP to their agents and get started from the terminal. They rarely want to log in and use the web UI themselves. We think developer tools must be agent-friendly to remain relevant.Here are some common findings that Gauge identifies:- agents get confused with CLI/SDK behavior and start source diving - interactive commands block agents - agents use deprecated/old CLI commands - agents don't use Skills when you'd expect -

items.author: One Useful Thing (Mollick)
items.title: 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts)
items.text:
30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts)
My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts.Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence, I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence, I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had th
